title: Money and inequality in Spain
lede: How much you earn, how much you pay, and how that compares with everyone else. An interactive exploration built on official data.
salary_prompt: How much do you earn? Pick the figure you know and let’s see where every euro goes.
salary_equivalents: That's {gross} gross per year: {net12} net per month over 12 payments, or {net14} over 14.
journey_lede: Out of every €100 gross, {socialSecurity} goes to Social Security, {irpf} to income tax (IRPF), and {net} reaches your account.
journey_slices_hint: Each orange slice is the IRPF paid by your euros on one step, labelled with its rate.
journey_effective: You pay {irpf} of IRPF a year: {rate} of your gross salary.
staircase_lede: Not all of your euros pay the same. Picture your salary as a row of euros, from the first to the last: the chart shows what takes a share of each one.
staircase_free: Your first {amount} pay no IRPF: they're covered by the work-income reductions and deductions and the personal allowance.
staircase_marginal: Your last euros pay {rate} in IRPF. That's your marginal rate: what you'd lose from each extra euro you earned.
staircase_hump: Look at the step between {from} and {to}: there, each extra euro pays up to {rate} in IRPF. It isn't a tax bracket.
staircase_label: How each euro of your gross salary is split, from the first to the last
tooltip_split: Of every €100 on this step: {socialSecurity} Social Security, {irpf} IRPF, and {net} for you.
children_shared_label: Does another parent share the child allowance?
assumption_individual: Individual filing, with no income other than your salary.
assumption_contract: A permanent contract, with extra payments prorated into the contribution bases.
assumption_final: This is the final tax for the year, not the withholding on each payslip.
assumption_deductions: Regional and foral deductions (rent, births…) and the maternity deduction aren't included.
hump_cause_common: It's where the work-income reduction and the minimum-wage deduction both phase out at once.
hump_cause_basque: It's where the work-income bonus (bonificación) phases out.
hump_cause_navarra: It's where the work deduction and the extra low-income personal deduction phase out.
assumption_children: Children count if they're under 25 (30 in the Basque Country and Navarre) with no income of their own.
cover_how: Six chapters, one after another, like squares on a board game. Start with your salary and everything after will be about you; or skip it and we'll use an example salary.
rail_label: Chapters and the salary in use
chapter_salary_teaser: From gross to net, euro by euro: who takes what.
chapter_history_teaser: Your salary under every IRPF scale since 1979.
chapter_inequality_teaser: Where you stand among wage earners, households and wealth.
chapter_evolution_teaser: Pay and inequality over the years, in today's euros.
chapter_capital_teaser: The same euros pay differently from work or from savings.

salary_optional: Right now we're using an example salary of {gross} gross a year. Change it to yours and every chapter will be about you. It stays in your browser and is never sent anywhere.
salary_personal: Done: the next chapters use your salary of {gross} gross a year.
history_intro: IRPF, Spain's income tax, was born in 1979 and its scale has changed many times since. Hop into the time machine: we turn each scale into today's euros (pesetas to euros, then corrected for inflation) and set it beside 2026's.
history_your_base: We're taking your taxable base along: {base}, what's left of your salary after Social Security and the work reductions.
history_example_base: We're taking the example salary's taxable base along ({gross} gross): {base}, what's left after Social Security and the work reductions.
history_chart_label: Marginal rate by taxable base, in today's euros, for the chosen year and for 2026
history_stat_tax: What the scale would take (today's euros)
history_story_1979: 1979: democracy's first IRPF. It had 28 brackets, from 15% to 65.51%, with a limit: the scale's tax couldn't exceed 40% of the base. And the family filed together, not each person.
history_story_1992: 1992: a new law let people file separately. Mid-year, a decree-law raised the scale to 56% to rein in the deficit. In 1997 the Constitutional Court ruled that a decree-law couldn't do that.
history_story_1999: 1999: the 1998 reform cut the top rate to 48% (39.6% state plus 8.4% regional) and created the personal and family minimum, the part of your pay that isn't taxed.
history_story_2007: 2007: the law still in force (with many changes) cut the scale to four brackets, topping out at 43%.
history_story_2012: 2012: in the crisis, a "complementary levy" added up to 7 points in 2012 and 2013. The top rate reached 52%.
history_story_2026: 2026: the state scale runs from 9.5% to 24.5% and each region adds its own on top, so the top rate depends on where you live.
history_caveat: Note: we only compare the scale. Each era had its own deductions, minimums and reductions, so the actual tax was different. In 1979 the scale applied to the whole family's income. For 2012 we use the state law's reference regional scale; each region could pass its own.
inequality_intro: Now let's look around. If we lined up everyone in Spain who earns a wage, from lowest to highest paid, where would you be?
parade_lede: Each column is a tenth of all wage earners ({year}), from lowest to highest paid, as tall as their mean gross yearly pay. Part-time workers are included.
parade_label: Mean gross yearly pay of each decile of wage earners, and the salary in use
parade_axis: Wage decile: 1 is the lowest-paid tenth; 10, the highest. The dashed line is the salary in use.
ruler_label: Where the salary falls among all wage earners
parade_you: A salary of {gross} gross a year beats {percent}% of wage earners.
parade_you_top: A salary of {gross} gross a year is in the best-paid 10%.
parade_median: Half of wage earners make less than {median} gross a year, and getting into the top 10% takes {top}.
parade_gap: The lowest-paid tenth earns {bottom} a year on average (many work part-time or part of the year); the highest-paid, {top}: about {times} times as much.
household_lede: But people live in households, not payslips. A salary that supports a family stretches less than the same salary for one person. Statistics account for this by dividing a household's net income by "consumption units": 1 for the first adult, 0.5 for each other adult and 0.3 for each child under 14. We compare with households in {year}.
household_other_income: Household's other net income per year
household_ruler_label: Where the household falls among all households
household_note: We count {children} children, the ones you entered in your personal situation (we assume they're under 14).
wealth_lede: Earning isn't owning. A household's wealth is what everything it owns is worth (home, savings, shares, businesses) minus what it owes. Press the button to switch from counting households to counting euros.
wealth_label: Households and their net wealth, by wealth group
wealth_reflect: The richest 10% of households own more than half of all wealth; the poorer half, less than a tenth. If Spain were 100 households with 100 coins, 10 households would have 53 coins and 50 households would have 8.
gini_lede: The Gini index sums up income inequality in one number: 0 if everyone had the same income and 100 if one person had it all.
gini_caption: Gini of disposable income per consumption unit. The vertical line marks Spain ({spain}). The axis starts at {from} so the differences show.
gini_yours: In your region the Gini is {yours}; in Spain, {spain} ({year} survey).
evolution_intro: One snapshot isn't enough. Has it got better or worse? Let's line up the wage earners again, this time letting the years run.
evolution_parade_lede: The same ten deciles, year by year, in today's euros. The dashed outlines are {from}: press play and watch how far each column moves from its shadow.
evolution_parade_label: Mean gross yearly pay of each decile of wage earners, in today's euros, for the chosen year
evolution_parade_axis: Pay in 2026 euros. Dashed outline: the same decile in {from}.
evolution_parade_reflect: Once inflation is taken out, nearly every column ends up close to its shadow: in two decades, what most salaries can buy has barely changed. In between, the 2008 crisis and the 2022 inflation pushed them down.
evolution_gini_lede: Household income inequality rose with the crisis, peaked in 2014 and has since fallen, with ups and downs.
evolution_gini_label: Gini index of Spain and of your region by survey year
evolution_gini_caption: Survey year; incomes are from the year before. Move the pointer over the chart to see each year.
evolution_top_lede: Surveys see the richest poorly. Tax records see them better: this is the share of all pre-tax income going to the top 10% of adults by income, and to the top 1%.
evolution_top_label: Share of pre-tax national income of the top 10% and top 1% by income, by year
evolution_top_reflect: For forty years, the top 10% has taken a bit more than a third of all income, and the top 1% around 11 or 12%: one part in nine for one person in a hundred.
capital_examples_title: Three ways to make ends meet
capital_examples_intro: Imagine three people. One earns the minimum wage; another owns three rented flats; the third receives dividends. Look at what comes in over a year, before expenses and taxes.
capital_examples_worker: A year working for minimum wage
capital_examples_wage: The 2026 minimum wage: {monthly} in each of 14 payments. Earning it means working throughout the year.
capital_examples_rent: Three homes at {monthly} per month each, occupied and paid for all 12 months. This is an illustrative amount you can change.
capital_examples_dividends: The same money coming in as from the three flats, paid out by shares instead. This requires invested capital and taking risk; it is not a guaranteed return.
capital_examples_ratio: The three flats bring in the equivalent of {ratio} annual minimum wages before expenses and taxes. Change the rent: how much does it take to match a year of work?
capital_examples_rental_tax: Rent comes with maintenance costs, possible mortgages and unpaid bills; we do not calculate its net profit here. For a private landlord, it falls under the general IRPF base, with deductible expenses and possible housing reductions. Dividends go into the savings base. The tax comparison below is between salary and savings income.
capital_intro: A euro doesn't pay the same everywhere it comes from. A salary pays Social Security and goes into IRPF's general scale. Dividends, interest and investment gains go to another scale, the savings scale, from 19% to 30%.
capital_reflect: On low salaries, the salary comes off better: the work reductions bring IRPF close to zero. From middling salaries it flips, and the gap widens the higher you go.
capital_curve_title: The whole ladder at a glance
capital_curve_label: Effective rate on the same amount as salary and as savings income, from 0 to 250,000 €
capital_curve_reflect: Each line is the total share the taxman (and Social Security, for salaries) takes from the same amount. Move the pointer to compare any amount.
capital_next: On a salary of {gross}, {extra} more as a raise would leave you {salary} net. The same {extra} as dividends or gains would leave you {savings}.
capital_caveat_employer: We don't count the employer's contribution, which doesn't come out of your payslip but is still a cost: around 30% of gross pay.
capital_caveat_benefits: Social Security isn't just a tax: it earns pension, unemployment and sick-leave rights.
capital_caveat_corporate: Dividends come out of profits that already paid corporate tax. And not all savings are taxed this way: pension plans, homes and other rules differ.
elections_pending: When the parties publish their programmes, we'll add their IRPF proposals here, each with its source, so you can see how each would affect you.
elections_intro: Meanwhile, play finance minister. Design your scale: how much is exempt, where each bracket starts and what rate it pays. Your salary and the ten wage deciles update instantly.
sandbox_stat_change_example: Change in the example's net pay
sandbox_deciles_lede: How much the mean salary of each wage decile would gain (or lose) a year with your scale. Blue: pays less IRPF than today. Orange: pays more.
sandbox_deciles_label: Change in yearly net pay of each wage decile with your scale
sandbox_caveat: Your scale replaces the state and regional ones together and applies to the taxable base; the work reductions and the minimum-wage deduction stay as today. We don't estimate how much the state would collect.
foral_note: The Basque Country and Navarra have their own savings rules, so here we calculate as if you lived in {region}, whose scale and minimums are the state's.
pay_amount_gross: per year, before tax and contributions
pay_amount_net: per payment, what reaches your account
